[spoiler=The user of the honey artifact and...what?] [b]Donji-Bok Seulbi[/b] is the current user of Musi-Kull, she is a current woman in service of the naval forces of Hyunseo,  but is currently on vacancy with a few members of her own men, plus a kid named [u]Guljeot[/u].
they were stationed in the rural village of Narimae, the place itself was small and about 1036 people, where lady Seulbi is, is in the Cafe, a simple rustic place, with the counter made of stone and wood, and the benches of the same material, the base being rock and the place to sit being wooden, while the shelves behind the counter also carried books.
Seulbi is a 46 years old short woman with a thin body and long dark brown tied hair, white skin and wearing a simple checkered light green shirt with a long blue skirt on her legs, and despite her age, her appearance seems very conserved for a woman with almost half a century old.
Hey Seulbi! Want to know what i will be when grow up?
The young kid said excited as he rolls himself in the spinning bench, she smiled at him sweetly, then asked him.
What is it, Gulji?The nickname she gave him, and then waited for his answer, which soon came.
I will become a admiral! Become a marine and go straight to the top!
That is a very nice dream Gulji, let me guess...They both started speaking together in a unique voice[b]a military admiral![/b]
She laughed a little, then looked to the little body, who finally stopped spining, then pinched his cheek and asked him:
So the little boy created by one of my men wish to become a admiral i see...when you grow up...She made a little pause, just to see Guljeot eyes shining like stars.I would love be part of your crew!
Her response immediately made the boy eyes get wider, he seemed excited and not even believing.
SERIOUSLY?!He yelled in excitement, at the same time almost falling from the bench, but Seulbi prevented it from happening by using her artifact power to grab his shirt and making her fingers stick on his dark shirt and then pulling him back, however, he did not showed any care for it and still focused on her wordsYOU REALLY ARE GOING TO JOIN MY SHIP WITH ALL YOUR UNIFORM AND POWERS?! YOU ARE GOING TO BE MY RIGHT HAND RIGHT WAY!
Seulbi launched him a soft smile, then answered his question sharing the boy excitement.
Of course i will, the same kid who is just learning how to tie his shoes now is promoting me to his first mate? What a honor...
As she took her hand off the boy's shirt, small traces of the translucent brighty yellow liquid remained, he however, did not cared much.
I will be admiral Gulji the most famous admiral with the largest crew on my ship! Everyone shall want to be aboard!
Everyone you say? She repeated his words as put her hand on her chin and raised a eyebrowSo i will be needing to dispute my position in your crew eh?
The boy cheeks became a little rubbish as she said, he then looked at her eyes and tried explain.
No! Not like that i mean , your position will be ir...irevo...ir, IMPOSSBLE TO REVOKE!
Irrevocable, GuljiShe corrected him while holding a laugh, then picked up a pot of oysters and put it on the counterHere, take some food, you need to be strong to my...great admiral!
The boy picked up the pot, his eyes shining as he saw the boiling oysters, he then thanked Seulbi, who then offered to him.
Want a but more flavor?
She said with her sweet smile, as the boy put his pot in front of her, she knew what should do, then turned her fingers into melting liquid honey, the liquid slowly falling into the oysters, with the boy looking with contained cheer every single drop of honey fall.
And...there you go!
Seulbi said as the final drop of honey hit the oyster, Guljeot naturally attacked the pot as soon it was all his.
[b]Munch munch munch[/b].
DELICIOUS!He affirmed as his tongue were passing around his lips to cleanEverything you make tastes...INCREDIBLE!
Seulbi observed him eating as a animal, touching her elbow on the counter told him.
Calm there big eater, otherwise you will be eating the whole pot!She joked as turned her eye side to one of her men to talk, fading her attention from the kid to her subordinates, one of them asked.
All these years on service, my lady, and still determined to serve not by logistic but my taking off the Jaysunim who commit crimes eh, that is resilience my ladyThe man drank a cup of raspberry juice in front of him, his lips a bit purpleBut, whatever, we have got a great Musijang for the government last mission, the Musi-Olingeo, it will surely...
[b]BLEGH[/b]
Guljeot felt a disgusting taste among the oysters, the crew immediately looked to him, one of the menhis own father, Juk-Sae Enggang was holding his back in case his kid was choking, he then picked up a piece of a oyster, it had spiral patterns in a black shell.
THIS THING IS ABSOLUTELY GROSS!
The entire cafe spitted whatever they were drinking or eating, then Seulbi immediately opened the boy's mouth to check, but it could no longer be taken away, she then looked at him, trying to keep herself calm while holding his shoulders.
Gulji, what you just ate is a artifact from the deep sea! A MusijangShe tried to breath more calmly, while also explainingEating that not only gives you rubber power and octopus like properties, BUT AS WELL THE INCAPACITY OF SWIMMING OR BEING AT OPEN SEA FOR TOO LONG!
She tried warning, but the kid seemed more desperate about the incapacity of swimming, then he screamed:
WHAAAT??!! I CAN NO LONGER SWIM??
He seemed angry rather crying, then the crew tried comfort him, while Seulbi was checking, his fingers were elastic, and stretching like rubber.
Hey look son, lady Seulbi is a great soldier and...
Liutnenant you mean.She corrected before cutting his talking, then started talking in a relatively calm voice toneLook, there is a total of 2 admirals, including the military one...
Guljeot spinned his bench to show his back to Seulbi,then said, with certain resignation.
Ok ok you won it YOU WONHe got off the benchNow i...need go to bathroom!
He said, as if he was pretending just to escape, Seulbi laughed a little, as one of her crewman, while devouring a bowl of rice said.
The boy need some time to explore his own ability lady Seulbi, let him discover by himself the incredible things he can doHe swollen the last piece of the bowlYou know, you are not so different, you also ate the Musi-Kull when young and just because it looked nice you ate!
She looked a little rubbish, but still looked to where the boy went and said.
Anyways, i see my vacancy will not he just about resting anymore, NEITHER YOURS MEN![/spoiler]

[i][b]Expansion Post[/b][/i]

[spoiler]

The northern region of Tirakan, often referred to as the southern plains, due to the comparatively unusual warm climate, the land stretching above the capital city Naerim, has long been a region of strategic and economic consequence to Tirakan, though its early identity often appears fragmented in surviving accounts. Prior to its incorporation into the Ignulid Kingdom, this region consisted of small but affluent city-states whose prosperity derived from controlling the cluster of mountain passes that connected the Tirak Valley with the northern plains. They essentially controlled the, at that time, only existing trade route from the Tirak Valley to the northern Hydronian Tribes, as passing through the mountains was impossible at those times. These cities were neither tribal nor militaristic in the classical sense of early Tirakan civilization, but they rather were mercantile enclaves that accumulated wealth through tariffs, caravan duties and a small-scale metallurgical production tied to the ore-bearing foothills that surrounded them. Although they depended heavily on trade with the Ignulid heartland to the south, they repeatedly resisted all attempts at political integration. This tension, rooted in conflicting priorities of autonomy and centralization, would eventually draw the attention of the Ignulid king Nebudnesir II during a crucial period of kingdom-building in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE. 
As the Ignulid kings consolidated their authority across the Tirak Valley, they encountered the limits of their influence in the far north. Royal scribes recorded frequent complaints from northern caravaneers about excessive tolls or arbitrary seizures and disputes that local councils refused to resolve according to the norms emerging under the Ignulid legal codes. The northern cities, in turn, viewed the rising kingdom with suspicion, believing that Nebudnesirs expansionist tendencies threatened their independence and profits. This dynamic created an increasingly unstable frontier, and despite their economic interdependence, the gulf between the policies of the southern monarchy and the practices of the northern councils widened year by year.
By approximately 610 BCE, conflicts became more openly hostile. Merchant guilds from Aruk and other Ignulid cities petitioned the crown to intervene, arguing that the northern cities were obstructing lawful trade, destabilizing prices, and in several instances violently detaining Tiraki traders who refused inflated customs. Surviving fragments from the Royal Archive refer to caravans being waylaid not by bandits but by the municipal guards of the very cities profiting from trade. To the Ignulid leaders, this behavior represented not merely economic friction but a challenge to royal legitimacy. Under the theological-political worldview of early Aelirianism, the king was the earthly steward of order sanctioned by the Four Dragons, and any polity obstructing lawful order implicitly challenged that divine mandate.
Tensions culminated during the reign of King Zigrabuk IV, the first king to standardize parchment for administrative cause and to radically centralize authority under his rule. When a diplomatic delegation sent by the king to negotiate standardized trade rules was turned away at the northern gate of the city of Marhal, the dismissal was interpreted as a deliberate affront to the crown. According to later chronicles, a messenger from Naerim carrying a proposal of mutual concessions was arrested by the council of Marhal and driven out under threat of death. Word of this insult reached Zigrabuk IV, and while historians debate the accuracy of dramatic embellishments added over centuries, the essential result is clear, as the king decided that peaceful integration had reached its limit.
An epos tells about, how in the early summer of 598 BCE, Zigrabuk IV ordered a northern campaign composed of veteran infantry from Aruk, siege engineers and local auxiliary forces familiar with the mountainous terrain. The strategy was precise. Rather than attempt to conquer the entire region at once, the king aimed to seize the largest and wealthiest of the city-states first. The assumption, proven correct, was that the smaller cities would abandon resistance once the dominant economic hub fell under Ignulid control.
The army marched north along the Tirak River, securing villages on the frontier that had previously shifted allegiance depending on which northern city held sway. To most of these settlements, the arrival of royal troops offered welcome relief from the fluctuating demands of the merchant councils. Chroniclers note that the march encountered little resistance until reaching the lower mountain passes, where scouts reported that Marhal had fortified its walls and mobilized its citizen militia. The king issued an ultimatum demanding submission, tribute, and integration into the kingdoms administrative order. The council of Marhal refused.
The siege of Marhal is one of the earliest recorded sieges in Tirakans military history described with any detail. Archaeological excavations at the site show clear evidence of wall reconstruction and layers of burnt debris corresponding to this period. The Ignulid forces encircled the city, cut off its aqueduct, and began building earthen ramps for siege towers, an indication of the kingdoms growing sophistication in warfare. While the defenders attempted several sorties, they lacked the discipline and equipment of the royal troops. After twelve days, the council reportedly fled during the night, perhaps in an attempt to negotiate or escape, leaving the population leaderless. With morale collapsing, the gates opened, and the city surrendered.
The fall of Marhal had immediate ripple effects throughout the northern highlands. The surrounding city-states had depended on Marhal as a diplomatic and commercial hub. Without its leadership, their political cohesion evaporated. Some sent emissaries offering submission. Others attempted to organize a defensive coalition but lacked the necessary trust and logistical coordination among themselves. Zigrabuk IV moved swiftly, dispatching detachments to each of these cities. In several cases, the mere arrival of royal troops was enough to secure peaceful surrender. Where resistance did occur, it was limited and poorly organized compared to the centralizing Ignulid army. Within three years, by approximately 595 BCE, the entirety of the northern corridor was under firm Ignulid authority.
Once the military phase concluded, the king implemented a comprehensive program of administrative integration. Rather than allowing the conquered cities to maintain their independent councils, he reorganized the region into two royal provinces, each overseen by a Nashir, a kind of steward, appointed directly from the capital. These stewards were responsible for tax collection, law enforcement, and the establishment of royal courts to replace the patchwork of mercantile legal systems that had previously governed trade disputes. Standardized weights, measures, and taxation schemes were introduced. Parchments found across the region bear identical markings to those used in Aruk, indicating uniform administration. Furthermore, the king stationed permanent garrisons at key crossroads, ensuring that rebellion would be difficult to organize and that trade caravans could travel safely without interference or extortion.
Part of the Ignulid strategy to secure long-term loyalty involved religious and cultural integration. Aelirianism, though already influential, had not yet fully permeated the northern cities, which traditionally worshipped river and mountain spirits. The monarchy, understanding the unifying power of religious identity, sponsored the construction of temples dedicated to the Four Dragons. These temples were essential centers of education, record-keeping and civic authority. Priests were dispatched to harmonize local traditions with state doctrine, assimilating rather than eradicating indigenous beliefs. By merging local customs into Aelirian symbology, the monarchy ensured cultural cohesion without provoking mass resistance.
The integration of the northern lands also required economic restructuring. While the regions wealth had historically been based on trade taxation, the Ignulid state shifted its economic role from gatekeeper to facilitator. Caravan routes were surveyed, repaired, and standardized. The monarchy declared that no city could impose arbitrary taxes, replacing the old system with predictable, kingdom-wide tariffs that encouraged long-distance merchants to use northern routes more heavily. This increased flow revitalized the regional economy under royal oversight. Warehouse districts, previously controlled by competing guilds, were reorganized under provincial administration with fixed fees. This not only increased royal revenues but also reduced corruption and price manipulation.
The assimilation process, although generally effective, did not occur without tension. Some northern elites who had profited under the old independent system opposed the new order. The Ignulid approach to dissent was firm but calculated. Those who resisted were removed from their positions, but many merchants were offered roles within the new economic structures. For example, records mention certain prominent trading families who were granted contracts to manage caravanserais or supply goods to the military, effectively turning former political opponents into stakeholders in the kingdoms stability.
Over time, the northern provinces became integral to the Ignulid state. Their strategic value, controlling access to the plains beyond, transformed them into buffer regions that protected the kingdom from potential threats. Their economic significance grew as the regulated trade routes increased wealth flow into Tirakan. By the late 6th century BCE, the settlement patterns, architectural remains, and recovered administrative parchments all show that the northern lands were fully adapted to the broader Ignulid system. Even the linguistic landscape shifted, as the dialects of the region adopted features of courtly Tiraki speech through the influence of royal schools and temple scribes. 
From 595 BCE onward, the northern highlands and passes remained continuously under Tiraki governance, surviving countless dynastic transitions, administrative reforms, and cultural transformations. When Naerim would later rise to prominence, built centuries after these events, it did so atop land already deeply woven into the kingdoms historical, political, and cultural fabric. The northern conquest ensured that the heartland and the frontier would forever be bound together by a shared administrative lineage that persisted into every era of Tirakans long history.
This continuity forms the basis of modern claims. The northern land has been part of the kingdoms territorial framework for more than two and a half millennia.
Today the plains are considered one of the countrys most economically indispensable zones, as it has developed into a strategic powerhouse that shapes nearly every sector of the unified state. Stretching along the wide arc above Naerim, the region contains two of Tirakans most important deep-water harbors, Nebrim and Al-Hambra, both of which serve as primary gateways for national exports and imports. These ports, heavily modernized in the late 20th century and gradually rebuilt throughout the civil war, now form the logistical backbone of the countrys industrial and energy sectors. Nearly all refined gas shipments, steel exports, container freight, and international cargo traffic move through these northern corridors, making the coastline one of the very busiest maritime zone in East Shamat.
Behind the coastline lies one of Tirakans most fertile agricultural belts. Generations of river sediment and a favorable climate created a landscape ideal for grain, fruit, and industrial crop production. Even during the long civil war, when other regions saw production collapse, the north managed to maintain relative agricultural output thanks to its naturally resilient soils and established cooperative system. In the reconstruction period today, the area is positioned to become the countrys leading supplier of domestic food security, allowing Naerims government to reduce reliance on imports and stabilize consumer prices. Irrigation upgrades, fertilizer supply chain reforms, and the introduction of mechanized farming, partly financed through foreign partnerships, are now transforming the region into a modern agro-industrial pillar.
Beyond agriculture and shipping, the north is also the central node of Tirakans gas industry. A dense network of pipelines, compressor stations, and refineries converges there, feeding the national grid as well as ports for international export. Most offshore gas from Kings Bay and the eastern shelves enters refinement through the northern corridor before being processed, liquefied, or distributed to domestic power plants. Because of this, the region represents not just economic value but strategic leverage in foreign diplomacy. It is one of the physical points where Tirakans energy wealth becomes globally relevant, and therefore an area undergoing accelerated expansion, both in terms of infrastructure and security presence.
Yet despite its strength, the region faces a growing demographic challenge. Since the end of the civil war, Naerim has become overwhelming attractive to young workers, engineers, students, and high-skill laborers. The capitals booming semiconductor sector, AI and drone research clusters, and new financial districts pull people southward, causing populations in northern towns to stagnate or decline. Some coastal cities operate at half the workforce they maintained a decade ago. Agricultural cooperatives increasingly rely on seasonal mobility programs to fill labor shortages, and even the gas industry reports gaps in technician availability. Local administrations warn that, without incentives or targeted resettlement programs, the region may struggle to maintain its critical output despite rising national demand.
